source: Suzgun et al. (2024) Belief in the Machine: Investigating Epistemological Blind Spots of Language Models
finding: KaBLE benchmark tests belief, knowledge and fact with epistemic-logic style tasks on 15 LLMs. Models do well on true statements but fail to affirm false first-person beliefs.
numbers: 13,000 questions, 13 tasks, 1,000 seed sentences (500 true, 500 false), 10 disciplines, 195,000 queries total. Fact verification: 85.7% true vs 74.5% false. First-person false belief confirmation 54.4% avg (true belief 92.1%). Third-person false belief about 80.7%.
quote: LMs struggle to affirm false beliefs, especially when expressed in the first person.
limits: Zero-shot, temperature 0, template ending in (A) Yes (B) No (C) Undeterminable. Soft-match scoring because some models broke format. Only names James and Mary.
agent_relevance: Belief claims should be checked separately from fact checks. An agent must hold 'user believes X' apart from 'X is true'.

source: Suzgun et al. (2024) Belief in the Machine: Investigating Epistemological Blind Spots of Language Models (factivity and recursion)
finding: Models lack a robust grasp that knowledge requires truth (factivity). Recursive knowledge (knows that knows) is weak.
numbers: Recursive verification 78.4%, confirmation 86.7% (true cases). Claude-3.5 Sonnet 35.8% on recursive verification. Models rarely pick 'undeterminable' for false knowledge claims: GPT-4o 6%, Claude-3.5 Sonnet 3.6%. Text and Table 2 differ on awareness (77.5% vs 89.7%).
limits: No consistent correlation between model size and performance. Authors say training-data causes are speculative.
agent_relevance: Add an explicit factivity check (K p implies p) before treating a claim as known.

source: Suzgun et al. (2024) KaBLE leaderboard page
finding: A public leaderboard for KaBLE exists. Seen only as a search result title, not read.
numbers: none read
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Could track newer models on epistemic tasks.

source: Sileo and Lernould (2023) MindGames: Targeting Theory of Mind in LLMs with Dynamic Epistemic Modal Logic
finding: Generates dynamic epistemic logic (muddy-children style) problems as entailment tasks with exact ground truth. Scale helps few-shot but not zero-shot.
numbers: 400 test cases, balanced True/False per setup, 4 setups (forehead-mud, mirror, thirst, explicit), 2-4 agents, order K=2. Two human NLP annotators: 94% accuracy, agreement 0.89 (most human errors: know whether vs know that). Pythia 70M-6.9B and GPT-3 ada-davinci: scaling improved 5-shot but not 0-shot. Spot check on 20 items: GPT-3.5 60%, GPT-4 70%.
limits: English templates only. Plain zero/few-shot prompting; authors note better prompting can change results. GPT-4 check is only 20 items.
agent_relevance: DEL problems can be generated and checked exactly. A clean test bed for an epistemic operator in the agent loop.

source: Sileo and Lernould (2023) MindGames, error analysis
finding: Failure mode: GPT-3.5 answers 'not enough information' and misses that a public announcement of ignorance carries information, as in muddy children.
numbers: GPT-3.5 inferred correctly only on very shallow items. GPT-4 solved the shown 2-person mirror example but erred on others.
limits: Qualitative; few samples.
agent_relevance: Treat 'someone did not know' as evidence, not as a null result.

source: Holliday, Mandelkern, Zhang (2024) Conditional and Modal Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Tests 29 LLMs on inference patterns with conditionals and epistemic modals (might, must). All make basic mistakes; zero-shot chain of thought helps a lot.
numbers: 29 LLMs, 20 instances per pattern, temperature 0 and 1, zero-shot, few-shot and zero-shot CoT. Zero-shot average correct on uncontroversial patterns ranges from 89% down to 45% across models. With CoT the best models reach near 90%.
quote: All the LLMs we tested make some basic mistakes with conditionals or modals
limits: One-step inferences; contested cases use human judgments reported in the literature, not new human data.
agent_relevance: CoT is a cheap fix for modal slips; still audit modal steps.

source: Holliday et al. (2024), overgeneralisation and inconsistency
finding: Many LLMs overgeneralise Modus Tollens, Disjunctive Syllogism and McGee-style modus ponens to modal and conditional cases, where humans see invalidity. Some models reject MT with 'might' yet accept MT with 'must', though the two are equivalent.
numbers: Best zero-shot models uniformly judge CMP (McGee) valid, contrary to humans; CoT improves this substantially but most still accept it at high rates. Inconsistent triads persist even when asked in one context window.
limits: Human judgments are from the literature.
agent_relevance: Shows pattern-matching to Boolean rules. A scaffold should flag modal embeddings explicitly.

source: Holliday et al. (2024), modal fallacies and benchmark correlation
finding: Almost all models accept invalid modal distribution over or (MuDistOr) and 'might A and might B so might (A and B)' (MiAg). They get duality (might not = not must) right. Scores correlate highly with Chatbot Arena, MMLU and GSM8K.
numbers: Correlation values are in Figure 6; not recorded here.
limits: Correlation across 29 models only.
agent_relevance: Duality is safe; distribution over disjunction is not. Use as a unit test for modal reasoning.

source: Holliday et al. (2024), material conditional point
finding: LLMs mostly reject contraposition and antecedent strengthening like humans, so they do not read 'if' as the material conditional. Scoring by the material analysis would wrongly count this as error.
numbers: Largely agree with human judgment (Appendices C.1.10-11).
limits: Qualitative summary.
agent_relevance: Evaluations must choose the right semantics first.

source: He et al. (2023) Hi-ToM: Higher-Order Theory of Mind Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Higher-order belief (belief about belief about belief) breaks LLMs. Accuracy falls as order rises and when agents lie.
numbers: Standard accuracy under 60% for all four LLMs. GPT-4-32k vanilla: 60.42 (no deception), 55.81 (deception), 58.11 overall; with CoT 59.88. Claude-instant 45.67 -> 46.33. GPT-3.5-turbo 27.50 -> 35.50 with CoT. Joint accuracy for GPT-4 at order 4 is about 0.1-0.15.
quote: CoTP prompting yields insignificant performance gains.
limits: Joint accuracy needs all lower-order answers right. Only 4 models, June 2023 versions.
agent_relevance: Recursive K operators are the weak point; handle depth by explicit nesting or a solver.

source: He et al. (2023) Hi-ToM, CoT and deception
finding: CoT did not help and could hurt when agents deceive. Authors guess longer chains amplify misleading info.
numbers: GPT-4 with deception: vanilla 55.81 vs CoT 55.72 (-0.09). Claude-instant with deception 42.00 -> 40.33 (-1.67). GPT-3.5 overall +8.00.
limits: The error-cascade explanation is a hypothesis.
agent_relevance: CoT is not a universal remedy for epistemic tracking.

source: Kim et al. (2023) FANToM: Stress-testing Machine Theory of Mind in Interactions
finding: Tests who-knows-what in information-asymmetric conversations with many question types per fact. Models pass the multiple-choice belief item but fail prerequisite who-knew list items: illusory ToM.
numbers: Human ALL score 87.5. GPT-4 0613 + CoT: ALL* 26.6 (June), 14.8 (Oct). ChatGPT + CoT 3.7. Llama-2 Chat + CoT 0.4. Fine-tuned Flan-T5 XL 53.7, below humans. Answerability list: GPT-4 June CoT 40.2 vs human 90.6; info access 57.7 vs 90.6.
quote: some instances of successful LLM ToM reasoning in FANTOM should be interpreted as illusory
limits: Strict consistency scoring. GPT-4 June vs October versions differ by about 12 points ALL*.
agent_relevance: Cross-checking one fact via several epistemic questions (who knows, who can answer, what does X believe) catches fake success.

source: Sclar et al. (2023) SymbolicToM: plug-and-play multi-character belief tracker
finding: A symbolic belief graph per character, nested to higher orders, used at decoding time, lifts LLMs on ToMi. An explicit epistemic structure combined with an LLM.
numbers: GPT-3-Davinci on ToMi +38 absolute points (92% averaged over question types). +62 points on first-order false-belief for Flan-T5-XL. +78 points on second-order false-belief for GPT-3.5. All models stay near-perfect on memory questions.
limits: ToMi has labelling ambiguities; authors add disambiguating sentences. Needs OpenIE and entailment pipeline; relies on story structure.
agent_relevance: Closest existing model of Kripke-style per-agent worlds inside an LLM pipeline. Explicit belief state beats prompting alone.

source: Sclar et al. (2023) SymbolicToM, robustness
finding: On paraphrased stories, supervised models collapse; a symbolic tracker plus off-the-shelf LLM does not.
numbers: ParaphrasedToMi: supervised TTT average accuracy drops 54 points; finetuned GPT3 loses about 40 points on false-belief questions on average.
limits: Uses a GPT3 module for the resulting-state step.
agent_relevance: Structured state generalises better than learned heuristics.

source: Ullman (2023) Large Language Models Fail on Trivial Alterations to Theory-of-Mind Tasks
finding: Small changes that keep the epistemic structure (a transparent container, so the character sees the contents) flip GPT-3.5 answers to wrong.
numbers: Transparent bag: GPT-3.5 still says Sam believes the bag is full of chocolate, P=95% (popcorn 0%).
quote: Isolated failure cases should count for more than average success rates
limits: Few hand-made vignettes; one model family (GPT-3.5). Author corrected an earlier misreport about a second prompt (double-space issue).
agent_relevance: Isolated failures count more than averages. Use perturbation tests on epistemic claims.

source: Kosinski (2023) Evaluating large language models in theory of mind tasks (PNAS 2024)
finding: Reports ToM-like success growing with model size; later work pushes back.
numbers: 40 false-belief tasks, 8 scenarios each (false belief, 3 true-belief controls, reversed versions); all 8 must be solved. 11 LLMs. Older models 0%. GPT-3 davinci-003 and ChatGPT-3.5: 20%. ChatGPT-4: 75%, matching 6-year-olds.
limits: Templates likely in training data. Shapira et al. rerun found GPT-3.5 lower than reported on one task.
agent_relevance: Baseline for pass rates before robustness checks.

source: Shapira et al. (2023) Clever Hans or Neural Theory of Mind?
finding: Across 6 tasks LLMs show some ToM but it is not robust; adversarial variants break them.
numbers: ToMi: GPT-3.5 81% overall but 46% on false-belief questions, near random. SocialIQa: GPT-4 79% total, lower on questions about others. Adv-CSFB: GPT-4 97.5% and 83.3% on two categories, with decline on others. Table 3 uses 400-instance samples.
quote: LLMs show some N-ToM abilities, but the behavior is far from being robust.
limits: Probing format changes scores (a 7 point difference for GPT-4 on SocialIQa).
agent_relevance: Report subset accuracy; false belief is the critical subset.

source: Strachan et al. (2024) Testing theory of mind in large language models and humans, Nature Human Behaviour
finding: Battery of ToM tests (false belief, irony, faux pas, hinting, strange stories) on GPT-4, GPT-3.5, LLaMA2-70B and humans. GPT-4 matched or beat humans on most but not faux pas.
numbers: 15 chats per model per test. False belief: ceiling for all. Irony: GPT-4 above humans (P=0.040, r=0.32); GPT-3.5 and LLaMA2-70B below. Faux pas: only 2 of 349 GPT-4 responses said the speaker knew.
quote: On the faux pas likelihood test GPT-4 demonstrated perfect performance
limits: Faux pas failure fits a hyperconservatism account: with a likelihood-framed question GPT-4 was perfect. Refusal to commit, not missing inference.
agent_relevance: 'Unclear' answers can be an epistemic-caution artifact. Ask for likelihood, not certainty.

source: Gandhi et al. (2023) Understanding Social Reasoning in Language Models with Language Models (BigToM)
finding: Procedural causal-template benchmark. GPT-4 mirrors human inference patterns, less reliably; other models struggle, especially with an explicit initial belief.
numbers: 25 controls and 5,000 model-written items; 20 Prolific human raters for baseline. Backward belief inference is hard even for humans: 82% true belief, 72% false belief.
limits: Human baseline n=20. Items written by an LLM.
agent_relevance: Backward inference (from actions to beliefs) is the hardest modal tracking step.

source: Xu et al. (2024) OpenToM
finding: Longer stories with personality and intent. LLMs model physical-world mental states well but fall short on psychological ones.
numbers: No numbers extracted; abstract-level read.
limits: Numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: Attitudes and preferences are harder than location beliefs.

source: Chen et al. (2024) ToMBench
finding: Bilingual multiple-choice benchmark, 8 tasks, 31 abilities, 10 LLMs. GPT-4 lags humans by over 10 points.
numbers: Gap to humans over 10 percentage points for GPT-4.
limits: Only abstract-level numbers captured.
agent_relevance: Contamination-resistant test set for ToM claims.

source: Pan et al. (2023) Logic-LM: Symbolic Solvers for Faithful Logical Reasoning
finding: LLM translates to symbolic form, a solver runs it, solver errors drive self-refinement. The pattern an epistemic solver tool would copy.
numbers: Average gain 39.2% over standard prompting and 18.4% over CoT. GPT-4 Standard/CoT/Logic-LM: PrOntoQA 77.4/98.8/83.2; ProofWriter 52.7/68.1/79.7; FOLIO 69.1/70.6/78.9; LogicalDeduction 71.3/75.3/87.6; AR-LSAT 33.3/35.1/43.0.
limits: First-order only, no modal datasets. On PrOntoQA GPT-4 CoT beats Logic-LM.
agent_relevance: Template for a modal solver tool: translate, solve, refine. Needs Kripke semantics.

source: Halpern and Moses (1990; arXiv 2000) Knowledge and Common Knowledge in a Distributed Environment
finding: Epistemic logic used to design distributed protocols; common knowledge tied to coordination (coordinated attack problem).
numbers: Formal; no empirical numbers.
limits: Theoretical, pre-LLM. Only the opening and a few passages read.
agent_relevance: Classic AI use of epistemic logic. Grounds 'everyone knows that everyone knows'.

source: Sileo and Lernould (2023) cite Moghaddam and Honey (2023) Boosting theory-of-mind performance in LLMs via prompting
finding: MindGames says this paper showed more advanced prompting made significant differences to ToM scores. Source paper not read.
numbers: none read
limits: Seen only as a citation.
agent_relevance: Prompt scaffolds may change epistemic scores; check before trusting zero-shot baselines.

source: Sileo and Lernould (2023) cite Dissing and Bolander (2020) Implementing ToM on a robot using DEL (IJCAI)
finding: Cited as a DEL implementation on a robot: an older AI system using epistemic logic. Not read.
numbers: none read
limits: Citation only; URL is the proceedings index.
agent_relevance: Prior art for DEL planning in agents.

source: Unverified probability-operator inference benchmark (alphaxiv 2607.27405, search snippet)
finding: Search snippet: tests inference over probability operators (probably, might, must), 14,320 prompts, 15 templates, gaps up to 64 points between logically identical items, partly from negation wording. Not verified.
numbers: 14,320 prompts; 15 templates; up to 64 point gaps (snippet only)
limits: Not opened; authors unknown; treat as unconfirmed.
agent_relevance: If real, supports wording-invariance checks for modals.

source: EpiK-Eval authors (2023) EpiK-Eval: Evaluation for Language Models as Epistemic Models
finding: Tests whether LMs form a consistent knowledge state from facts spread over separate documents. They fail to consolidate, behave like Type I systems and hallucinate more.
numbers: 18 tasks x 100 stories = 1,800 stories; 6,800 segments; 1,800 QA pairs. T5/Flan-T5 small to XL and OPT 125M-2.7B. Models trained on unsegmented stories clearly beat segmented-trained ones. Train hallucination at most 0.2%. Exact test accuracies not in text read.
quote: LMs struggle to consolidate knowledge from multiple sources
limits: Small models only; leakage risk so release is encrypted.
agent_relevance: Write facts into one consolidated belief state rather than rely on scattered notes.
